prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

No classes here! Why, that is idle talk. The village beau sneers at the country boor; The importuning mendicants who walk Our cites’ streets despise the parish poor. The daily toiler at some noisy loom Holds back her garments from the kitchen aid. Meanwhile the latter leans upon her broom, Unconscious of the bow the laundress made. The grocer’s daughter eyes the farmer’s lass With haughty glances; and the lawyer’s wife Would pay no visits to the trading class, If policy were not her creed in life. The merchant’s son nods coldly at the clerk; The proud possessor of a pedigree Ignores the youth whose father rose by work; The title-seeking maiden scorns all three. The aristocracy of blood looks down Upon the “nouveau riche”; and in disdain, The lovers of the intellectual frown On both, and worship at the shrine of brain. “No classes here,” the clergyman has said; “We are one family.” Yet see his rage And horror when his favorite son would wed Some pure and pretty player on the stage. It is the vain but natural way Of vaunting our weak selves, our pride, our worth! Not till the long delayed millennial day Shall we behold “no classes” on God’s earth.

outputs.L1:
“No classes here!” Why, that is idle talk.  
The village beau sneers at the country boor;  
The importuning mendicants who walk  
Our city streets despise the parish poor.  

The daily toiler at some noisy loom  
Holds back her garments from the kitchen aid;  
Meanwhile, the latter leans upon her broom,  
Unconscious of the bow the laundress made.  

The grocer’s daughter eyes the farmer’s lass  
With haughty glances; and the lawyer’s wife  
Would pay no visits to the trading class  
If policy were not her creed in life.  

The merchant’s son nods coldly at the clerk;  
The proud possessor of a pedigree  
Ignores the youth whose father rose by work;  
The title-seeking maiden scorns all three.  

The aristocracy of blood looks down  
Upon the “nouveau riche”; and, in disdain,  
The lovers of the intellectual frown  
On both, and worship at the shrine of brain.  

“No classes here,” the clergyman has said;  
“We are one family.” Yet see his rage  
And horror when his favorite son would wed  
Some pure and pretty player on the stage.  

It is the vain but natural way  
Of vaunting our weak selves, our pride, our worth;  
Not till the long-delayed millennial day  
Shall we behold “no classes” on God’s earth.
outputs.L2:
“Class distinctions do not exist here!” Such a claim is nonsense. The admired young man of the village mocks the rough country fellow, while persistent beggars roaming city streets look down on the poor who depend on the parish. A woman who labors daily at a clattering loom draws her clothing away from the kitchen servant; at the same time, the servant rests on her broom, not noticing the slight bow made by the laundress.

The grocer’s daughter regards the farmer’s girl with proud contempt, and the lawyer’s wife would never call on people in trade if social strategy were not part of her way of living. The merchant’s son gives only a chilly nod to the clerk. The person who takes pride in an old family line refuses to acknowledge the young man whose father gained position through hard work, while the girl who longs for a title looks down on all three of them.

Those who prize noble blood disdain the newly wealthy; and, in turn, those who value intellect above all else frown upon both groups and make the mind their object of reverence. “There are no classes among us,” the minister declares. “We are all one family.” But observe his fury and shock when his beloved son wishes to marry a virtuous and lovely actress.

This is the empty yet very human habit of exaggerating our own importance, dignity, and superiority. Only when the long-awaited millennium finally arrives will humanity truly see a world without classes on God’s earth.
outputs.L3:
The poem argues that social class is a universal reality, even in places where people claim that “there are no classes here.” Although society may present itself as democratic or equal, the poem suggests that divisions of rank, occupation, wealth, and status continue to shape how people think about one another.

One of the main points of the poem is that people often look down on those they consider beneath them. This attitude is not limited to the rich or powerful. People from many different occupations and social positions judge others according to their work, income, manners, or background. Each group tends to find someone else to feel superior to, creating a chain of prejudice throughout society.

The poem also emphasizes that class prejudice exists among both the wealthy and the working classes. It is not only aristocrats or upper-class people who hold snobbish views. Ordinary workers, tradespeople, and members of the middle class can also show contempt for those they regard as lower in status. In this way, the poem presents social prejudice as a widespread human habit rather than a problem belonging to one class alone.

Another important idea is the hypocrisy of people who publicly support equality but privately maintain class distinctions. Even those who preach democratic values or speak against privilege may reveal bias in their personal lives, especially in matters such as friendship, marriage, and social respectability. Their actions show that their belief in equality is often limited or inconsistent.

The poem concludes on a pessimistic but thoughtful note. It suggests that a truly classless society does not yet exist and may only become possible in some ideal future age. Until people overcome their desire to rank themselves above others, social classes and class prejudice will continue to survive, despite claims that everyone is equal.
outputs.L4:
The poem argues against the comforting claim that society has “no classes” by showing how deeply class feeling appears in ordinary life. Instead of treating class as something limited to formal ranks or inherited titles, the poem presents it as a habit of comparison that runs through every level of society. People look down on others because of their occupations, their manners, their money, their family background, their education, or their claims to respectability. Even those who are themselves looked down upon often find someone else to regard as inferior. In this way, social snobbery becomes not merely a feature of the wealthy or powerful, but a common human weakness.

Through its catalog of examples, the poem exposes the contradictions behind the belief in a classless society. A person may deny that class distinctions matter while still judging others by the kind of work they do, the neighborhood they live in, the clothes they wear, or the refinement they appear to possess. Wealth may create one hierarchy, pedigree another, intellect another, and moral reputation yet another. The poem suggests that people are endlessly inventive in finding reasons to separate themselves from others and to claim some small superiority.

By the end, the poem’s tone becomes skeptical and ironic. It does not simply condemn one particular social group; instead, it suggests that class prejudice is rooted in human vanity itself. The desire to feel above someone else persists even when political or social language insists on equality. Therefore, true social equality is presented as a noble ideal rather than a present reality. The poem concludes that a world without such distinctions may not arrive until some far-off “millennial day,” a distant future when human pride and snobbery have finally disappeared.

**Why The Our Matters**

Why do we search for meaning in the things around us? The answer often begins with our own experiences, our choices, and our hopes for the future. The world is full of questions, and each one gives us a chance to understand ourselves better.

Our lives are shaped by the people we meet, the lessons we learn, and the dreams we follow. When we ask “why,” we open the door to curiosity and growth. The more we explore, the more we discover what truly matters.

In the end, our journey is not only about finding answers, but also about appreciating the questions that guide us forward.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a satirical poem in a 19th-century style mocking the claim that there are “no classes here,” showing many subtle forms of social snobbery in American life.
counterfactuals.output:
**“No Classes Here”**

“No classes here!” the trumpet cries,  
Beneath the courthouse dome;  
The eagle spreads impartial wings  
Above each equal home.  
The cobbler nods, the banker smiles,  
The parson wipes a tear—  
A blessed land, a level land:  
There are no classes here.

No classes—yet the front pew knows  
The perfume of its own;  
The poorer saints may praise the Lord,  
But softly, and alone.  
The velvet cushion takes its ease,  
The pine bench holds its cheer;  
All souls are weighed alike in Heaven—  
But not, precisely, here.

No classes—yet at Mrs. Sprague’s  
The callers rise by grade;  
The silver teapot tilts itself  
Where pedigrees are laid.  
A hand may shake a merchant’s hand,  
If trade has made it clear  
That cotton, coal, or pork enough  
Can cleanse a grandsire here.

No classes—yet the boarding school  
Has mysteries of birth;  
The boys compare their fathers’ names,  
The girls their mothers’ worth.  
One learns to pause before a “Smith,”  
To smile upon a “Vere”;  
The alphabet is common law—  
But not all letters here.

No classes—yet the village ball  
Receives with careful grace;  
The grocer’s daughter dances once,  
Then finds a cooling place.  
The judge’s niece is passed like wine,  
The widow’s child like beer;  
The fiddle scrapes democracy—  
But rank selects the ear.

No classes—yet the railway car,  
So proudly “public,” shows  
A certain frost around the man  
Whose collar’s out of pose.  
His boots have argued with the mud,  
His coat is plain and sere;  
The cushions are republican—  
The glances less so, here.

No classes—yet the hotel clerk,  
That sentinel of fate,  
Can read a fortune in a trunk  
And estimate a plate.  
A shabby valise waits humbly by,  
A steamer chest draws near;  
The register is open wide—  
But ink flows finer here.

No classes—yet the summer shore  
Has fences made of air;  
The bathing hour, the porch, the chair,  
Declare who may be where.  
The waves arrive in equal troops,  
Each foam-capped pioneer;  
But even Ocean learns, by August,  
Whom it should revere.

No classes—yet the wedding cards  
Are sifted like the wheat;  
Some neighbors send sincere regrets  
From just across the street.  
The bridegroom’s uncle made his pile,  
The bride’s great-aunt was “dear”;  
Love conquers all, the papers say—  
Except the list, my dear.

No classes—yet the clubroom doors  
Have hinges shrewd and thin;  
They swing for “men of character,”  
Which means, for men let in.  
The blackball drops, a little moon  
Eclipsing a career;  
All citizens may smoke at home—  
But not Havanas here.

No classes—yet the kitchen hears  
What drawing-rooms deny;  
The maid observes who must be “miss,”  
And who is “that young fly.”  
The butler knows the nation’s soul,  
The coachman knows its gear;  
The republic rides in livery—  
But calls the harness “mere.”

No classes—yet the graveyard slopes  
In terraces of pride;  
The marble angels congregate  
On one expensive side.  
The pauper’s field has equal dust,  
The sexton’s price is clear;  
Death levels all, as preachers say—  
With lots more level here.

“No classes here!” the trumpet cries,  
And long may it be blown;  
It sweetens trade, it oils the tongue,  
It makes the boast our own.  
For we have barred the ancient gate  
And burned the courtier’s spear—  
Then built a hundred smaller gates  
And named them “custom,” here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a rhymed Victorian-style poem about class distinctions, beginning with the phrase “No classes here!” and ending with the idea that true equality will only come in a millennial age.
counterfactuals.output:
“No classes here!”—the placard cried,  
Above the feast, the hall, the mart;  
Yet velvet brushed the worker’s side,  
And silver chilled the beggar’s heart.  

The lord in broadcloth bowed full low,  
The clerk replied with careful grace;  
But still the hidden lines would show  
In hand, in accent, and in place.  

The maid might tread the marble stair,  
The master praise her honest worth;  
Yet one possessed the house and air,  
And one but hired her hour on earth.  

They spoke of rights with polished ease,  
Of brotherhood, of common bread;  
While hunger shivered in the breeze,  
And plenty’s lamp burned gold o’erhead.  

O England, robed in smoke and song,  
With chapel-bell and factory chime,  
How long shall birth exalt the strong,  
And need be counted half a crime?  

Still dream we must, and strive, and pray,  
Till pride and want alike are past;  
For true equality waits the day—  
The millennial age, when all are classed at last.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: I need a poem that exposes hypocrisy around social equality: people say society has no classes, but everyone looks down on someone else. Use examples like merchants, clerks, clergy, actors, aristocrats, and the nouveau riche.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Ladder We Deny**

They tell us class is over now,  
a relic, rusted, dead—  
no ranks beneath the Sunday hat,  
no crowns above the head.  
“We’re equal here,” the speeches say,  
“one people, side by side,”  
while every smile is measuring  
the distance left to hide.

The merchant weighs his neighbor’s worth  
like sugar on a scale,  
and praises honest enterprise  
while mocking those who fail.  
The clerk, with ink upon his cuffs,  
looks down on hands of grime,  
and calls his little desk a throne  
from nine to closing time.

The clergy preach humility  
beneath a vaulted roof,  
then dine with donors, nodding grave,  
and keep the poor aloof.  
The actor bows to common love,  
then turns from common faces,  
and saves his sweetest practiced grin  
for wealth in velvet places.

The lord laments that titles fade,  
that “breeding” is ignored,  
yet trembles when new money knocks  
and buys what he adored.  
The newly rich, with chandeliers,  
with silver still too bright,  
laugh loudest at the rented rooms  
they slept in just last night.

So down the ladder each one peers,  
and upward each one sighs;  
we curse the boot upon our necks,  
then polish boots our size.  
No classes? Then why all these masks,  
this careful social art—  
the bowed head, raised brow, guarded door,  
the velvet, sneering heart?

Equality is praised in ink,  
in hymn, in stage, in trade;  
but every banquet has its edge,  
and every welcome, grade.  
We say no one is lesser here,  
no blood is blue or base—  
then find, in every human crowd,  
someone to put in place.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a formal, old-fashioned satirical verse in iambic meter about social hierarchy and class prejudice, with the refrain or central claim “No classes here.”
counterfactuals.output:
**No Classes Here**

Good sirs, behold our equal town,  
Where every man may bow and cheer;  
The lord looks kindly, leaning down,  
And whispers, “No classes here.”

The merchant’s wife, with gracious smile,  
Receives the poor—if clean, sincere;  
They wait outside the gate awhile:  
She murmurs, “No classes here.”

The parson praises lowly birth,  
Yet keeps the pews by rank and tier;  
“All souls,” quoth he, “are equal worth—  
Most surely, no classes here.”

The judge, in wig and scarlet gown,  
Bids beggars hold the law in fear;  
For gold may stand, but rags sit down:  
“Observe, lads, no classes here.”

At feasts, the servants glide unseen,  
While gentlefolk their consciences clear;  
The wine is red, the linen clean,  
And all toast, “No classes here.”

So hail the land of open doors,  
Where none are low, and none severe;  
Except, of course, the rich—and poor—  
But bless us, no classes here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem as if by Ella Wheeler Wilcox criticizing the denial of class divisions, using rhyming couplets/quatrains and a moralizing final stanza.
counterfactuals.output:
They say, “There is no class, no wall,  
No lordly height, no lowly hall;  
One common road for all men lies  
Beneath the same impartial skies.”

Yet one is born where roses lean  
Across a lawn forever green;  
And one where smoke and hunger meet,  
And childhood shivers in the street.

They say, “The race is fair and free;  
Who wills to rise, shall surely be.”  
But some start forth with golden wings,  
And some with chains and wounded things.

The banquet glitters in the light,  
The kitchen toils beyond the sight;  
And still the well-fed lips declare  
That want is but a lack of prayer.

O foolish heart, that will not see  
The ranks and roads of poverty!  
O blinded pride, that names as “chance”  
The old injustice of circumstance!

No peace is built on pleasant lies,  
No truth is slain because it cries;  
Who calls the bitter waters sweet  
But leaves the poison at his feet.

Then lift the veil, and speak the shame;  
Give grief its station and its name.  
For only he who sees the chain  
Can help to break the links in twain.

And this the law by Heaven planned:  
That strength shall serve the weaker hand;  
Till justice walks where sorrow trod,  
And brotherhood is truth with God.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
